To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) informational engagements about social media initiatives reflect multiple organizing visions; (b) informational engagements about a firm’s social media initiatives reflect the same schemas as the informational engagements about social initiatives of other firms; (c) the schemas reflected in a firm’s informational engagements are not necessarily the same across all of a firm’s social initiatives; (d) informational engagements that are not about social media initiatives are not necessarily about the same schemas as informational engagements about social-media initiatives.
(a) firms’ informational engagements reflect schemas that reflect different organizing visions; and (b) firms’ informational engagement about social media typically reflects multiple visions.
firms' informational engagements about social media reflect multiple organizing visions, and these visions can be summarized by six evaluative principles.
In summary, our research is concerned with
how the pluralism of organizing visions is reflected in firms’ informational engagements about social media and the implications of this pluralism for the value that firms garner from social media.
the pluralism of schemas that underlie firms’ information engagements, and we offer a framework for understanding and classifying schemas in terms of evaluative principles.
the pluralistic nature of organizing visions and their constitutive evaluative elements, and we offer relational class analysis as an empirical technique for surfacing schemas.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the schemas or visions of firms’ informational engagements about social media are not singular and not necessarily consistent.
the schemas identified are the result of the interplay of the social and technical aspects of the social media initiatives.
social media is a tool that can help firms achieve their business objectives, but it can be used in different ways, and firms should choose the way that best suits their objectives.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social construction of social media in firms is not a simple process, and it is not a process where there is only one way to see it.
the schemas of firms’ informational engagements about social media are not as singular as the extant literature suggests.
the informational engagements about social media are more complex than what has been previously theorized.
The main takeaway from our work is that
schemas, as opposed to single organizing visions, underlie firms’ information engagements.
the organizing vision of a technology is not necessarily unitary, but can be pluralistic, and that the pluralism can be observed through the schemas that underlie informational engagements.
firms’ informational engagements about social media reflect multiple visions, not a single vision.
